title: The divergence-graph edge algorithm for equal-length horocyclic suffixes: linear-time certification of close successors and computation of the uncancelable clique by a finite-state machine
author: Noah Jillson, Daniel N. Levitin, Pramana Saldin, Katerina Stuopis, Qianruixi Wang, Kaicheng Xue
work: Finite-State Machines for Horospheres in Hyperbolic Right-Angled Coxeter Groups
difficulty_reason: The counted proof is the paper's own correctness argument for the finite-state machine that decides divergence-graph edges between horocyclic suffixes of equal length, and it is not a qualification exercise. Even with the standing assumptions, the horocyclic normal form of Section 5.1 and the cancellation lemmas of Section 5.2 supplied, the author has to build the state - the subwords u_1, u_2 and u_3, u_4 (or u_5, u_6) of the two horocyclic suffixes, the clique K of uncancelable letters, the bit b recording which word owns the cancelable letters, and the two subword indices n_w and n_v - and then verify five interlocking update rules: the index update, the bit flip forced when one word has moved on to a later subword, the adding letter, the processing of the canceling letter together with the deletion of the letters that it forbids, and the closing bit-flip check. The mathematical content is the invariant maintained across those rules, that K is always a clique commuting with every surviving subword, and the two-sided conclusion: any failure of a check is exactly a pair of uncancelable letters, while a successful run computes K(v,w), the word of cancelable letters, and the side of the pair on which that word must be written. Nothing here is a textbook computation: it is the paper's own reduction of the geometry of the divergence graph to a finite automaton over the horocyclic normal form, and it is what makes the article's later linear-time and O(n log n) generation theorems work. This is research-level geometric group theory and automata over Coxeter groups, well beyond an ordinary PhD qualifying examination.
